items.title: Quiz Q#251 · Matthew Prior
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Matthew Prior
items.stem: Which major 1709 poetic collection (expanded into a lavish folio in 1718) established Matthew Prior’s reputation as an Augustan master of light society verse, philosophical tales, and polished epigrams?
options: The Hind and the Panther Transvers’d
A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: Matthew Prior's 'Poems on Several Occasions' (1709/1718) contained some of the finest occasional verse and humorous philosophical poems of the Augustan age, including 'Alma; or, The Progress of the Mind'.

items.explanation: Jonathan Swift's 'The Battle of the Books' (1704) intervened in the Phalaris controversy on behalf of Sir William Temple, celebrating the ancients who, like bees, provide 'the two noblest of things, which are sweetness and light'.

items.stem: Which 1714 sequence of six pastorals in heroic couplets by John Gay parodied Ambrose Philips by presenting gritty, rustic English farm life with authentic dialect and folklore?
items.explanation: Intended by Pope and Gay as a satirical attack on Ambrose Philips's idealized pastorals, Gay's 'The Shepherd's Week' (1714) unexpectedly delighted readers with its charming depiction of real English country customs.

items.title: Quiz Q#323 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Gay does the character of The poet (A guide who sings the art of walking London) appear?
items.explanation: The poet is a prominent figure in John Gay's Trivia, characterized as a guide who sings the art of walking london.

items.title: Quiz Q#324 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Through winter streets to steer your course aright"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Gay's Trivia (1716).

items.title: Quiz Q#325 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem: Which 1716 mock-georgic poem in heroic couplets by John Gay, subtitled 'The Art of Walking the Streets of London', offers an encyclopedic, humorous guide to early 18th-century London street hazards?
items.explanation: Gay's 'Trivia' (1716) adapts Virgil's 'Georgics' to the urban landscape, warning pedestrians against pickpockets, coach mud, chimney sweeps, and gutter hazards with vibrant satirical realism.

items.title: Quiz Q#326 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Gay does the character of The Hare (A polite animal deserted by many so called friends) appear?
items.explanation: The Hare is a prominent figure in John Gay's Fables, characterized as a polite animal deserted by many so called friends.

items.title: Quiz Q#327 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"And when a lady's in the case"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Gay's Fables (1727).

items.title: Quiz Q#328 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem: Which 1727 collection of moral beast fables in octosyllabic couplets by John Gay, written for the young Prince William, satirized court corruption and sycophancy through animal tales like 'The Hare and Many Friends'?
items.explanation: John Gay's 'Fables' (1727; second series posthumous 1738) achieved international popularity for their graceful wit, moral clarity, and subtle political digs at Sir Robert Walpole's administration.

items.title: Quiz Q#329 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Gay does the character of Peachum (A receiver of stolen goods who informs on weaker thieves) appear?
items.explanation: Peachum is a prominent figure in John Gay's The Beggar’s Opera, characterized as a receiver of stolen goods who informs on weaker thieves.

items.title: Quiz Q#330 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"How happy could I be with either"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in John Gay's The Beggar’s Opera (1728).

items.title: Quiz Q#331 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem: Which revolutionary 1728 ballad opera by John Gay, produced by John Rich at Lincoln's Inn Fields, satirized Italian opera and Prime Minister Robert Walpole through the highwayman Captain Macheath?
items.explanation: John Gay's 'The Beggar's Opera' (1728) was a legendary triumph that 'made Gay rich and Rich gay', substituting popular street ballad melodies for aristocratic Italian recitative and exposing society's criminal elite.

items.title: Quiz Q#332 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem: In which landmark work by John Gay does the character of Polly Peachum (Macheath's wife, sold as a servant in the West Indies) appear?
items.explanation: Polly Peachum is a prominent figure in John Gay's Polly, characterized as macheath's wife, sold as a servant in the west indies.

items.title: Quiz Q#333 · John Gay
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · John Gay
items.stem: Which 1729 ballad opera sequel by John Gay was banned from theatrical performance by the Lord Chamberlain due to its political satire, but became a bestselling printed text?
items.explanation: Following Polly Peachum to the West Indies to rescue Macheath, Gay's 'Polly' (1729) was censored by Prime Minister Walpole's orders, generating massive publicity and financial profit in print.

items.title: Quiz Q#334 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem: In which landmark work by Alexander Pope does the character of The poet-critic (Pope speaking as a young critic of critics) appear?
items.explanation: The poet-critic is a prominent figure in Alexander Pope's An Essay on Criticism, characterized as pope speaking as a young critic of critics.

items.title: Quiz Q#335 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"A little learning is a dangerous thing"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Alexander Pope's An Essay on Criticism (1711).

items.title: Quiz Q#336 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem: Which 1711 didactic verse essay in heroic couplets established 23-year-old Alexander Pope as a major critical voice, formulating classic maxims like 'A little learning is a dang’rous thing' and 'To err is human, to forgive divine'?
items.explanation: Pope's 'An Essay on Criticism' (1711) codifies Neoclassical literary principles derived from Horace and Boileau, urging critics to 'Follow Nature' and align sound with sense in poetry.

items.title: Quiz Q#337 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem: In which landmark work by Alexander Pope does the character of The poet (Pope, arguing for order in the universe) appear?
items.explanation: The poet is a prominent figure in Alexander Pope's An Essay on Man, characterized as pope, arguing for order in the universe.

items.title: Quiz Q#338 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Whatever is, is right"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Alexander Pope's An Essay on Man (1733-1734).

items.title: Quiz Q#339 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem: Which 1733–1734 philosophical poem in four epistles by Alexander Pope seeks to 'vindicate the ways of God to man', exploring the Great Chain of Being and concluding that 'Whatever is, is right'?
items.explanation: Dedicated to Lord Bolingbroke, Pope's 'An Essay on Man' (1733–1734) outlines an Enlightenment rationalist theodicy, examining man's place in the universe, human nature, society, and the pursuit of happiness.

items.title: Quiz Q#340 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem: In which landmark work by Alexander Pope does the character of Dulness (The goddess who spreads bad writing and empty thought) appear?
items.explanation: Dulness is a prominent figure in Alexander Pope's The Dunciad, characterized as the goddess who spreads bad writing and empty thought.

items.title: Quiz Q#341 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"And universal darkness buries all"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Alexander Pope's The Dunciad (1728).

items.title: Quiz Q#342 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem: Which four-book mock-heroic masterpiece by Alexander Pope chronicles the reign of the goddess Dulness spreading intellectual darkness over Great Britain, crowning Lewis Theobald and later Colley Cibber as king?
items.explanation: Alexander Pope's 'The Dunciad' (1728; final four-book edition 1743) attacks Grub Street hacks, bad publishers, and political patronage, culminating in the terrifying vision: 'And universal Darkness buries All'.

items.title: Quiz Q#343 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem: In which landmark work by Alexander Pope does the character of Belinda (The heroine, based on Arabella Fermor) appear?
items.explanation: Belinda is a prominent figure in Alexander Pope's The Rape of the Lock, characterized as the heroine, based on arabella fermor.

items.title: Quiz Q#344 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"What mighty contests rise from trivial things"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Alexander Pope's The Rape of the Lock (1712).

items.title: Quiz Q#345 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem: Which consummate mock-heroic poem in heroic couplets by Alexander Pope elevates a trivial society quarrel over a severed lock of hair into an epic contest featuring sylphs, gnomes, and the Cave of Spleen?
items.explanation: Alexander Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock' (published in 2 cantos in 1712 and expanded to 5 cantos in 1714) satirizes fashionable London high society by applying Homeric epic machinery to Belinda and the Baron.

items.title: Quiz Q#346 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem: In which landmark work by Alexander Pope does the character of Achilles (The angry hero who opens Pope's Iliad) appear?
items.explanation: Achilles is a prominent figure in Alexander Pope's translations of Homer, characterized as the angry hero who opens pope's iliad.

items.title: Quiz Q#347 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Achilles' wrath, to Greece the direful spring"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Alexander Pope's translations of Homer (1715-1726).

items.title: Quiz Q#348 · Alexander Pope
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Alexander Pope
items.stem: Which monumental verse translation in heroic couplets published by subscription between 1715 and 1726 gave Alexander Pope lifelong financial independence and was praised by Johnson as 'a performance which no age or nation can pretend to equal'?
items.explanation: Pope's translations of Homer's 'Iliad' (1715–1720) and 'Odyssey' (1725–1726, with William Broome and Elijah Fenton) rendered ancient Greek epic into fluent, elegant Augustan heroic couplets.

items.title: Quiz Q#349 · Samuel Richardson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Richardson
items.stem: In which landmark work by Samuel Richardson does the character of Pamela Andrews (The young maid whose letters and journal tell the story) appear?
items.explanation: Pamela Andrews is a prominent figure in Samuel Richardson's Pamela, characterized as the young maid whose letters and journal tell the story.

items.title: Quiz Q#350 · Samuel Richardson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Richardson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"That he had not offer'd the least Indecency"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Samuel Richardson's Pamela (1740).

items.title: Quiz Q#351 · Samuel Richardson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Richardson
items.stem: Which 1740 landmark epistolary novel by Samuel Richardson, subtitled 'Virtue Rewarded', follows the virtuous 15-year-old maidservant Pamela Andrews as she resists the advances of her master Mr. B?
items.explanation: Samuel Richardson's 'Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded' (1740) was a cultural sensation that pioneered the psychological epistolary technique ('writing to the moment'), sparking the Pamela controversy and Henry Fielding's parodies.

items.title: Quiz Q#352 · Samuel Richardson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Richardson
items.stem: In which landmark work by Samuel Richardson does the character of Clarissa Harlowe (The virtuous heroine who dies rather than accept a false peace) appear?
items.explanation: Clarissa Harlowe is a prominent figure in Samuel Richardson's Clarissa, characterized as the virtuous heroine who dies rather than accept a false peace.

items.title: Quiz Q#353 · Samuel Richardson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Richardson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"The History of a Young Lady"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Samuel Richardson's Clarissa (1747-1748).

items.title: Quiz Q#354 · Samuel Richardson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Richardson
items.stem: Which monumental 1747–1748 epistolary tragic novel by Samuel Richardson, running to over a million words, chronicles the abduction, violation, and saintly death of Clarissa Harlowe at the hands of the rake Lovelace?
items.explanation: Richardson's 'Clarissa; or, The History of a Young Lady' (1747–1748) is widely regarded as his greatest psychological masterpiece, staging an intense moral duel between Clarissa's spiritual integrity and Lovelace's destructive libertinism.

items.title: Quiz Q#355 · Samuel Richardson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Richardson
items.stem: In which landmark work by Samuel Richardson does the character of Sir Charles Grandison (The good gentleman whose duty and kindness solve the plot) appear?
items.explanation: Sir Charles Grandison is a prominent figure in Samuel Richardson's Sir Charles Grandison, characterized as the good gentleman whose duty and kindness solve the plot.

items.title: Quiz Q#356 · Samuel Richardson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Richardson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"A good man and fine gentleman"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Samuel Richardson's Sir Charles Grandison (1753-1754).

items.title: Quiz Q#357 · Samuel Richardson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Samuel Richardson
items.stem: Which 1753 epistolary novel by Samuel Richardson was designed to present a paragon of male Christian virtue and benevolence, contrasting with the libertine villainy of Lovelace and Mr. B?
items.explanation: In 'The History of Sir Charles Grandison' (1753), Richardson created an idealized Christian gentleman torn between his love for the English heroine Harriet Byron and his moral obligations to the Italian Catholic Clementina della Porretta.

items.title: Quiz Q#358 · Henry Home, Lord Kames
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Henry Home, Lord Kames
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"derived from the human heart"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Henry Home, Lord Kames's Elements of Criticism (1762).

items.title: Quiz Q#359 · Henry Home, Lord Kames
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Henry Home, Lord Kames
items.stem: Which influential 1762 three-volume treatise on aesthetics by the Scottish philosopher Lord Kames sought to base literary criticism upon the psychological laws of human nature rather than arbitrary classical rules?
options: Sketches of the History of Man
Essays on the Principles of Morality and Natural Religion
items.explanation: Lord Kames's 'Elements of Criticism' (1762) became a foundational text of the Scottish Enlightenment and rhetorical theory, analyzing human emotions and perception to explain literary aesthetic responses.

items.title: Quiz Q#360 · Lord Kames / Henry Home
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Lord Kames / Henry Home

options: Sketches of the History of Man
Essays on the Principles of Morality and Natural Religion
items.explanation: Lord Kames's 'Elements of Criticism' (1762) became a foundational text of the Scottish Enlightenment and rhetorical theory, analyzing human emotions and perception to explain literary aesthetic responses.

items.title: Quiz Q#361 · Anne Finch
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Anne Finch
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"In such a night, when every louder wind"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anne Finch's A Nocturnal Reverie (1713).

items.title: Quiz Q#362 · Anne Finch
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Anne Finch
items.stem: Which 1713 meditative poem in heroic couplets by Anne Finch, praised by William Wordsworth for its rare and genuine observation of night-time nature, describes twilight sounds and grazing horses?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: Anne Finch's 'A Nocturnal Reverie' (1713) stands out among Augustan poems for its vivid sensory appreciation of the nocturnal countryside, prefiguring later Romantic celebrations of quiet natural solitude.

items.title: Quiz Q#363 · Anne Finch
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Anne Finch
items.stem: In which landmark work by Anne Finch does the character of The speaker (A sufferer who addresses melancholy as if it were a living power) appear?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: The speaker is a prominent figure in Anne Finch's The Spleen, characterized as a sufferer who addresses melancholy as if it were a living power.

items.title: Quiz Q#364 · Anne Finch
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Anne Finch
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"What art thou, Spleen"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Anne Finch's The Spleen (1701).

items.title: Quiz Q#365 · Anne Finch
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Anne Finch
items.stem: Which 1701 Pindaric ode by Anne Finch explores the 18th-century affliction of melancholy and nervous depression, depicting the mental anguish and creative frustration of the sufferer?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: Anne Finch's 'The Spleen, a Pindaric Ode' (1701) offers an incisive, personal diagnosis of the fashionable 18th-century ailment of melancholy, analyzing its physical symptoms and psychological effects on women writers.

items.title: Quiz Q#366 · James Thomson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Thomson
items.stem: In which landmark work by James Thomson does the character of The speaker (A meditating voice that watches the changing year) appear?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: The speaker is a prominent figure in James Thomson's The Seasons, characterized as a meditating voice that watches the changing year.

items.title: Quiz Q#367 · James Thomson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Thomson
items.stem: Which celebrated blank-verse nature poem published in four parts between 1726 and 1730 by James Thomson ('Winter', 'Summer', 'Spring', 'Autumn') revitalized nature poetry in English literature?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: James Thomson's 'The Seasons' (1726–1730) combined Miltonic blank verse with scientific observation of the natural world and religious awe, exerting massive influence on pre-Romantic and Romantic sensibilities.

items.title: Quiz Q#368 · James Thomson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Thomson
items.stem: In which landmark work by James Thomson does the character of Indolence (The wizard who traps guests in luxurious idleness) appear?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: Indolence is a prominent figure in James Thomson's Castle of Indolence, characterized as the wizard who traps guests in luxurious idleness.

items.title: Quiz Q#369 · James Thomson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Thomson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"As heav'n and earth they would together mell"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in James Thomson's Castle of Indolence (1748).

items.title: Quiz Q#370 · James Thomson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Thomson
items.stem: Which 1748 two-canto allegorical poem by James Thomson, written in Spenserian stanzas, depicts an enchanted castle where a wizard lulls mortals into luxurious lethargy until overcome by the Knight of Industry?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: Thomson's 'The Castle of Indolence' (1748) was one of the finest 18th-century imitations of Edmund Spenser, masterfully using the Spenserian stanza to evoke dreamy sensory languor in Canto I and active industry in Canto II.

items.title: Quiz Q#371 · James Thomson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Thomson
items.stem: In which landmark work by James Thomson does the character of The speaker (A wanderer in a city and a desert of despair) appear?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: The speaker is a prominent figure in James Thomson's The City of Dreadful Night, characterized as a wanderer in a city and a desert of despair.

items.title: Quiz Q#372 · James Thomson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Thomson
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"No hope could have no fear"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in James Thomson's The City of Dreadful Night (1874).

items.title: Quiz Q#373 · James Thomson
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · James Thomson
items.stem:
Which major 18th-century work by James Thomson matches the following form and literary characteristics?
"It does not fit this author. James Thomson of The Seasons died in 1748. The City of Dreadful Night is by James Thomson (Bysshe Vanolis), born in 1834. It ran in the National Reformer in 1874 and in a book in 1880."
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: This description highlights James Thomson's The City of Dreadful Night, an influential landmark in 18th-century English literature.

items.title: Quiz Q#374 · Lady Mary Wortley Montagu

items.explanation: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu is a prominent figure in Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's Turkish Embassy Letters, characterized as the traveler who writes the letters.

items.title: Quiz Q#375 · Lady Mary Wortley Montagu

items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"The small-pox, so fatal, and so general"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's Turkish Embassy Letters (1763).

items.title: Quiz Q#376 · Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Lady Mary Wortley Montagu
items.stem: Which posthumously published 1763 collection of letters by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu challenged European orientalist stereotypes by providing an insider account of Ottoman society, baths, and smallpox inoculation?
options: A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: Written during her husband's embassy to Constantinople in 1716–1718 and printed in 1763, Lady Mary's 'Turkish Embassy Letters' provided a sympathetic, secular, and proto-feminist view of Turkish women and culture.

items.title: Quiz Q#377 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin
items.stem: In which landmark work by Benjamin Franklin does the character of Benjamin Franklin (The narrator, telling his own rise) appear?
items.explanation: Benjamin Franklin is a prominent figure in Benjamin Franklin's Autobiography written 1771–1790, characterized as the narrator, telling his own rise.

items.title: Quiz Q#378 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"three great Puffy Rolls"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Benjamin Franklin's Autobiography written 1771–1790 (1791).

items.title: Quiz Q#379 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin
items.stem: Which classic autobiographical memoir, begun in 1771 and published in 1791, details the author’s rise from a humble printer’s apprentice to world-renowned statesman through a program of 13 moral virtues?
items.explanation: Benjamin Franklin's 'Autobiography' established the archetype of the self-made individual, detailing his printer career, scientific discoveries, civic projects, and systematic plan for moral perfection.

items.title: Quiz Q#380 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin
items.stem: In which landmark work by Benjamin Franklin does the character of Richard Saunders (The made up author, a man who claims to read the stars) appear?
items.explanation: Richard Saunders is a prominent figure in Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack, characterized as the made up author, a man who claims to read the stars.

items.title: Quiz Q#381 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"God helps those who help themselves"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanack (1732).

items.title: Quiz Q#382 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin
items.stem: Which annual American colonial publication issued between 1732 and 1758 under the pseudonym Richard Saunders popularized hundreds of practical proverbs on thrift, industry, and prudence?
items.explanation: Franklin's 'Poor Richard’s Almanack' was widely read across colonial America, collecting aphorisms later synthesized in 'The Way to Wealth' ('Early to bed and early to rise...').

items.title: Quiz Q#383 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin
items.stem: In which landmark work by Benjamin Franklin does the character of Benjamin Franklin (The experimenter writing from Philadelphia) appear?
items.explanation: Benjamin Franklin is a prominent figure in Benjamin Franklin's Experiments and Observations on Electricity, characterized as the experimenter writing from philadelphia.

items.title: Quiz Q#384 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Nothing in this Way of Use to Mankind"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Benjamin Franklin's Experiments and Observations on Electricity (1751).

items.title: Quiz Q#385 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin
items.stem: Which groundbreaking 1751 scientific work by Benjamin Franklin proved the electrical nature of lightning through his famous kite experiment and introduced the terms positive and negative charge?
items.explanation: Franklin's 'Experiments and Observations on Electricity' (1751) won him global scientific acclaim and the Royal Society's Copley Medal, establishing the single-fluid theory of electricity and inventing the lightning rod.

items.title: Quiz Q#386 · Benjamin Franklin
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Benjamin Franklin

items.explanation: Benjamin Franklin is a prominent figure in Benjamin Franklin's Autobiography, characterized as the narrator of his own unfinished life.

items.explanation: Benjamin Franklin's 'Autobiography' established the archetype of the self-made individual, detailing his printer career, scientific discoveries, civic projects, and systematic plan for moral perfection.

items.title: Quiz Q#389 · Henry Fielding
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Henry Fielding
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"An apology for Mrs. Shamela Andrews"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Henry Fielding's Shamela (1741).

items.title: Quiz Q#390 · Henry Fielding
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Henry Fielding
items.stem: Which hilarious 1741 epistolary parody by Henry Fielding, published under the pseudonym Conny Keyber, burlesqued Samuel Richardson’s 'Pamela' by depicting the heroine as a scheming, calculating hypocrite?
items.explanation: Fielding's 'An Apology for the Life of Mrs. Shamela Andrews' (1741) exposed what he viewed as the prurience and mercenary virtue of Richardson's 'Pamela', renaming the characters Shamela and Squire Booby.

items.title: Quiz Q#391 · Henry Fielding
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Henry Fielding

items.explanation: Joseph Andrews is a prominent figure in Henry Fielding's Joseph Andrews, characterized as a chaste footman, presented as pamela's brother.

items.title: Quiz Q#392 · Henry Fielding

items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"A comic epic poem in prose"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Henry Fielding's Joseph Andrews (1742).

items.title: Quiz Q#393 · Henry Fielding
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Henry Fielding
items.stem: Which 1742 novel by Henry Fielding, defined in its famous preface as a 'comic epic poem in prose' written in the manner of Cervantes, follows the travels of a chaste footman and Parson Abraham Adams?
items.explanation: Henry Fielding's 'Joseph Andrews' (1742) evolved from a parody of Richardson's 'Pamela' into a vibrant social picaresque, celebrating the unworldly benevolence of Parson Adams across the English road.

items.title: Quiz Q#394 · Henry Fielding
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Henry Fielding
items.stem: In which landmark work by Henry Fielding does the character of Tom Jones (The warm hero Allworthy raises, later found to be of gentle birth) appear?

items.title: Quiz Q#463 · Adam Smith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Adam Smith
items.stem: In which landmark work by Adam Smith does the character of Adam Smith (The author, arguing in his own voice as a moral philosopher) appear?
items.explanation: Adam Smith is a prominent figure in Adam Smith's The Theory of Moral Sentiments, characterized as the author, arguing in his own voice as a moral philosopher.

items.title: Quiz Q#464 · Adam Smith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Adam Smith
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"How selfish soever man may be supposed"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Adam Smith's The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759).

items.title: Quiz Q#465 · Adam Smith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Adam Smith
items.stem: Which 1759 moral philosophy treatise by Adam Smith posits that human morality and social conscience are rooted in mutual 'sympathy' and evaluated by an internal 'impartial spectator'?
items.explanation: In 'The Theory of Moral Sentiments' (1759), Adam Smith argued that ethical judgments emerge from imaginative sympathy with others' feelings rather than mere self-interest, introducing the concept of the 'impartial spectator'.

items.title: Quiz Q#466 · Adam Smith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Adam Smith
items.stem: In which landmark work by Adam Smith does the character of Adam Smith (The author, explaining markets, wages, and the duties of the state) appear?
items.explanation: Adam Smith is a prominent figure in Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations, characterized as the author, explaining markets, wages, and the duties of the state.

items.title: Quiz Q#467 · Adam Smith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Adam Smith
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"led by an invisible hand"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776).

items.title: Quiz Q#468 · Adam Smith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Adam Smith
items.stem: Which foundational 1776 economic work by Adam Smith analyzed the division of labor, free trade, and the self-regulating power of competitive markets guided by an 'invisible hand'?
items.explanation: Adam Smith's 'An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations' (1776) established modern classical economics, advocating free enterprise and criticizing mercantilist trade restrictions.

items.title: Quiz Q#469 · Frances Brooke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Frances Brooke
items.stem: In which landmark work by Frances Brooke does the character of Emily Montague (The shy heroine whose love for Rivers shapes the plot) appear?
options: The History of Lady Julia Mandeville
items.explanation: Emily Montague is a prominent figure in Frances Brooke's The History of Emily Montague, characterized as the shy heroine whose love for rivers shapes the plot.

items.title: Quiz Q#470 · Frances Brooke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Frances Brooke
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"It is a painful consideration, my dear"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Frances Brooke's The History of Emily Montague (1769).

items.title: Quiz Q#471 · Frances Brooke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Frances Brooke
items.stem: Which 1769 epistolary work by Frances Brooke, set in Quebec shortly after the British conquest, is widely recognized as the earliest novel written in and about Canada?
options: The History of Lady Julia Mandeville
items.explanation: Frances Brooke's 'The History of Emily Montague' (1769) blends romantic sentimentality with vivid eyewitness descriptions of Canadian landscapes, Quebec winter life, and Native American culture.

items.title: Quiz Q#472 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: In which landmark work by Oliver Goldsmith does the character of Dr Charles Primrose (The vicar who narrates the story) appear?
items.explanation: Dr Charles Primrose is a prominent figure in Oliver Goldsmith's The Vicar of Wakefield, characterized as the vicar who narrates the story.

items.title: Quiz Q#473 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Such qualities as would wear well"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Oliver Goldsmith's The Vicar of Wakefield (1766).

items.title: Quiz Q#474 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: Which beloved 1766 domestic novel by Oliver Goldsmith recounts the Job-like trials, financial misfortunes, and enduring Christian patience of Dr. Charles Primrose and his family?
items.explanation: Oliver Goldsmith's 'The Vicar of Wakefield' (1766) combines sentimental domestic comedy with gentle satire of the unworldly vicar's naivety, remaining one of the most popular 18th-century novels.

items.title: Quiz Q#475 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: In which landmark work by Oliver Goldsmith does the character of The traveller (The speaker, looking over Europe from the Alps) appear?
items.explanation: The traveller is a prominent figure in Oliver Goldsmith's The Traveller, characterized as the speaker, looking over europe from the alps.

items.title: Quiz Q#476 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Our own felicity we make or find"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Oliver Goldsmith's The Traveller (1764).

items.title: Quiz Q#477 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: Which 1764 philosophical poem in heroic couplets by Oliver Goldsmith, subtitled 'A Prospect of Society', surveys the national characters, politics, and social happiness of Italy, Switzerland, France, and England?
items.explanation: Oliver Goldsmith's 'The Traveller' (1764) established his poetic reputation, using balanced heroic couplets to argue that true human happiness depends upon individual virtue rather than forms of government.

items.title: Quiz Q#478 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: In which landmark work by Oliver Goldsmith does the character of Honeywood (The good natured hero whose kindness is a fault) appear?
items.explanation: Honeywood is a prominent figure in Oliver Goldsmith's The Good-Natur’d Man, characterized as the good natured hero whose kindness is a fault.

items.title: Quiz Q#479 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"I now too plainly perceive my errors"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Oliver Goldsmith's The Good-Natur’d Man (1768).

items.title: Quiz Q#480 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: Which 1768 stage comedy by Oliver Goldsmith satirized the excesses of indiscriminate benevolence through the character of young Honeywood and featured the comic hypochondriac Mr. Croaker?
items.explanation: Goldsmith's 'The Good-Natur'd Man' (1768) attempted to rescue English comic theater from the weeping sentimentality of Hugh Kelly, although its realistic bailiff scene initially shocked genteel audiences.

items.title: Quiz Q#481 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: In which landmark work by Oliver Goldsmith does the character of The speaker (A poet who mourns the lost village of Auburn) appear?
items.explanation: The speaker is a prominent figure in Oliver Goldsmith's The Deserted Village, characterized as a poet who mourns the lost village of auburn.

items.title: Quiz Q#482 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Sweet Auburn, loveliest village of the plain"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Oliver Goldsmith's The Deserted Village (1770).

items.title: Quiz Q#483 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: Which poignant 1770 social poem in heroic couplets by Oliver Goldsmith laments the destruction of rural English peasantry and agricultural communities due to the Parliamentary Enclosure Acts and mercantile greed?
items.explanation: Goldsmith's 'The Deserted Village' (1770) mourns the fictional village of 'Sweet Auburn, loveliest village of the plain', warning against the concentration of luxury at the expense of dispossessed rural laborers.

items.title: Quiz Q#484 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: In which landmark work by Oliver Goldsmith does the character of Kate Hardcastle (The daughter who stoops to a barmaid's dress to win Marlow) appear?
items.explanation: Kate Hardcastle is a prominent figure in Oliver Goldsmith's She Stoops to Conquer, characterized as the daughter who stoops to a barmaid's dress to win marlow.

items.title: Quiz Q#485 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"I love everything that's old"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Oliver Goldsmith's She Stoops to Conquer (1773).

items.title: Quiz Q#486 · Oliver Goldsmith
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: Which brilliant 1773 'laughing comedy' by Oliver Goldsmith centers on young Marlow’s shyness around aristocratic ladies and Kate Hardcastle’s stratagem of posing as a barmaid to win his love?
items.explanation: Oliver Goldsmith's 'She Stoops to Conquer' (1773), subtitled 'The Mistakes of a Night', championed robust laughing comedy over weeping sentimentalism through characters like Tony Lumpkin and Mrs. Hardcastle.

items.title: Quiz Q#487 · Edmund Burke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Edmund Burke
items.stem: In which landmark work by Edmund Burke does the character of Edmund Burke (The author, sorting the causes of aesthetic feeling) appear?
options: A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful
Reflections on the Revolution in France
Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents
items.explanation: Edmund Burke is a prominent figure in Edmund Burke's A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful, characterized as the author, sorting the causes of aesthetic feeling.

items.title: Quiz Q#488 · Edmund Burke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Edmund Burke
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"I have great reason to doubt"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Edmund Burke's A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757).

items.title: Quiz Q#489 · Edmund Burke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Edmund Burke
items.stem: Which foundational 1757 aesthetic treatise by Edmund Burke separated the Beautiful (rooted in social pleasure and smoothness) from the Sublime (rooted in terror, obscurity, and vastness)?
options: Reflections on the Revolution in France
Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents
A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful
items.explanation: Burke's 'A Philosophical Enquiry' (1757) had a profound impact on Kant, Gothic literature, and Romanticism by identifying the Sublime with emotions of awe, danger, and self-preservation.

items.title: Quiz Q#490 · Edmund Burke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Edmund Burke
items.stem: In which landmark work by Edmund Burke does the character of Edmund Burke (The writer, a Whig who breaks with admirers of the Revolution) appear?
options: A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful
Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents
Reflections on the Revolution in France
items.explanation: Edmund Burke is a prominent figure in Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, characterized as the writer, a whig who breaks with admirers of the revolution.

items.title: Quiz Q#491 · Edmund Burke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Edmund Burke
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Society is indeed a contract"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790).

items.title: Quiz Q#492 · Edmund Burke
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · Edmund Burke
items.stem: Which landmark 1790 political treatise by Edmund Burke attacked the violent radicalism of the French Revolution and championed traditional institutions, gradual reform, and hereditary monarchy?
options: A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful
Reflections on the Revolution in France
Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents
items.explanation: Edmund Burke's 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' (1790) ignited the Revolutionary Controversy in Britain, provoking famous rebuttals from Thomas Paine, Mary Wollstonecraft, and William Godwin.

items.title: Quiz Q#493 · William Cowper
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Cowper
items.stem: In which landmark work by William Cowper does the character of The worshipper (The voice of the hymns, a believer praying, doubting, and hoping) appear?
items.explanation: The worshipper is a prominent figure in William Cowper's Olney Hymns (with John Newton), characterized as the voice of the hymns, a believer praying, doubting, and hoping.

items.title: Quiz Q#494 · William Cowper
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Cowper
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"God moves in a mysterious way"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Cowper's Olney Hymns (with John Newton) (1779).

items.title: Quiz Q#495 · William Cowper
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Cowper
items.stem: Which 1779 hymn collection co-authored by William Cowper and the curate John Newton contributed beloved spiritual classics to the English language, including 'Amazing Grace' and 'God moves in a mysterious way'?
items.explanation: The 'Olney Hymns' (1779) emerged from the Evangelical Revival, containing 68 hymns by Cowper reflecting his intense spiritual devotion and recurring anxieties of divine abandonment.

items.title: Quiz Q#496 · William Cowper
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Cowper
items.stem: In which landmark work by William Cowper does the character of The poet speaker (Cowper himself, talking through walks, winter scenes, and reflections) appear?
items.explanation: The poet speaker is a prominent figure in William Cowper's The Task, characterized as cowper himself, talking through walks, winter scenes, and reflections.

items.title: Quiz Q#497 · William Cowper
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Cowper
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"God made the country"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Cowper's The Task (1785).

items.title: Quiz Q#498 · William Cowper
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Cowper
items.stem: Which major 1785 six-book poem in blank verse by William Cowper began as a playful challenge to write about a parlor sofa and expanded into a celebrated meditation on country life, abolitionism, and natural piety?
items.explanation: Cowper's 'The Task' (1785) established conversational blank verse as a medium for intimate reflection, containing the famous line 'God made the country, and man made the town' and deeply influencing Wordsworth's 'The Prelude'.

items.title: Quiz Q#499 · William Cowper
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Cowper
items.stem: In which landmark work by William Cowper does the character of The poet speaker (Cowper, judging the manners and writing of his age) appear?
items.explanation: The poet speaker is a prominent figure in William Cowper's Poems, characterized as cowper, judging the manners and writing of his age.

items.title: Quiz Q#500 · William Cowper
items.meta: The Long Eighteenth Century · William Cowper
items.stem:
Who is the author of the work containing the following famous line or critical statement?
"Poor England! thou art a devoted deer"
items.explanation: This famous line appears in William Cowper's Poems (1782).
